title: How do you choose a partition key, and what happens if you choose badly (hot partition)?
shortTitle: Choosing a partition key and what happens with a bad choice (hot partition)

s1_definition.profdef: A partition key is the value Kafka hashes to decide which partition of a topic a record is written to. Records with the same key always land in the same partition, which gives per-key ordering. A good key is one with high cardinality and even distribution so load spreads across all partitions. A bad key has low cardinality or heavy skew, so a disproportionate share of records funnels into one partition. That overloaded partition is a hot partition: its single consumer and single broker leader become a bottleneck while other partitions sit idle.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture National Bank of India with twelve teller windows (partitions). The key is the rule that decides which window a customer goes to. If you send customers by account id, which is unique and spread out, all twelve windows stay evenly busy. But if you send them by branch city and ninety percent of customers are from Mumbai, one window has a giant queue while eleven windows are empty. That one jammed window is the hot partition — the whole bank feels slow even though it has twelve windows.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pick a high-cardinality, evenly distributed key so load spreads across all partitions; a skewed key creates a hot partition that bottlenecks one consumer and one broker.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A partition key is the value Kafka hashes to decide which partition of a topic a record is written to. Records with the same key always land in the same partition, which gives per-key ordering. A good key is one with high cardinality and even distribution so load spreads across all partitions. A bad key has low cardinality or heavy skew, so a disproportionate share of records funnels into one partition. That overloaded partition is a hot partition: its single consumer and single broker leader become a bottleneck while other partitions sit idle.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture National Bank of India with twelve teller windows (partitions). The key is the rule that decides which window a customer goes to. If you send customers by account id, which is unique and spread out, all twelve windows stay evenly busy. But if you send them by branch city and ninety percent of customers are from Mumbai, one window has a giant queue while eleven windows are empty. That one jammed window is the hot partition — the whole bank feels slow even though it has twelve windows.

**One line to remember:** Pick a high-cardinality, evenly distributed key so load spreads across all partitions; a skewed key creates a hot partition that bottlenecks one consumer and one broker.

sections.s2_technical:
Kafka chooses the partition with the formula `partition = murmur2(key) % numPartitions` for the default partitioner when a key is present. Because the same key always hashes to the same partition, keying by account id guarantees that all events for one account are processed in order on one partition. That ordering guarantee is the main reason to use a key at all in a bank, where the sequence of debits and credits for an account must be preserved.

Choosing the key is a balance between two goals: ordering and distribution. You want enough ordering to be correct and enough spread to use all partitions. A customer id or account id is usually a good choice because there are millions of them and traffic is roughly even. A key like country, status, or a boolean flag is usually a bad choice because there are only a few distinct values, so records pile into a few partitions.

A hot partition shows several symptoms. The consumer lag for that one partition climbs while others stay near zero. One broker that leads the hot partition shows high CPU and disk use. Throughput for the whole topic is capped by that one partition because a partition is processed by exactly one consumer in a group. Adding more consumers does not help because they cannot subdivide a single partition.

When the key must stay for ordering but one key is naturally huge, there are senior techniques. You can use a composite key such as account id plus a small bucket number, which spreads one very active account across a few partitions while still grouping most traffic. You can increase the partition count, though that reshuffles key-to-partition mapping and only helps if the skew is across many keys, not one dominant key. You can write a custom `Partitioner` that applies business logic, for example sending known high-volume merchant accounts to dedicated partitions. In Spring, you set the key simply by using the key argument: `kafkaTemplate.send("transfers", account.getAccountId(), event)`.

The caution in banking is that if you ever relax the key to improve distribution, you may lose per-account ordering, which can cause a credit to be processed before the matching debit. So you only spread a key when you can tolerate the ordering change for that slice of traffic.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India publishes every transfer to a transfers topic with twelve partitions. The team first keyed records by the two-letter region code. There are only four regions and most traffic is from the West region, so one partition took the majority of records. That partition's consumer fell far behind while three partitions were almost empty. This is exactly a hot partition caused by a low-cardinality key.

Problem 2 — The team switched the key to account id. Now there are millions of distinct keys and traffic spreads evenly across all twelve partitions, so no single consumer is overloaded and per-account ordering is still preserved. This is exactly how a high-cardinality key fixes skew.

We simulate both choices in plain Java. A `Partitioner` computes `hash(key) % partitions`, and we feed the same set of transfers once keyed by region and once keyed by account id, then count records per partition to reveal the skew. The code will show: the `Transfer` event, a `BankPartitioner` using murmur2-like hashing, and a demo that prints the distribution for both key choices so the hot partition is visible.

```yaml
# application.yml — real producer keyed by account id for per-account ordering
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    producer:
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonSerializer
      properties:
        partitioner.class: org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.internals.DefaultPartitioner
# Topic "transfers" created with 12 partitions.
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: 10000 transfers where 90 percent carry region WEST, and each has a unique account id.

Step 1: The producer first keys by region. The partitioner hashes WEST to one partition. Because 90 percent of records are WEST, that one partition receives roughly 9000 records.

Step 2: The remaining three regions spread across a few other partitions, and most of the twelve partitions receive zero records. The distribution array shows one huge bucket and many empty buckets.

Step 3: The consumer group assigns one consumer per partition. The consumer on the WEST partition must process 9000 records while ten other consumers sit idle, so lag on that partition climbs and overall throughput is capped.

Step 4: The producer switches to key by account id. Each of the 10000 unique account ids hashes independently, so records spread roughly evenly across all twelve partitions, about 830 per partition.

Step 5: Now every consumer has a similar load, lag stays low, and per-account ordering is still guaranteed because each account id always maps to the same partition.

```
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [WARNING] Keyed by REGION (low cardinality) -> [0,0,0,9023,0,0,412,0,301,0,264,0]
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [SEVERE ] Hot partition detected: one partition holds most records.
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] Keyed by ACCOUNT ID (high cardinality) -> [835,829,841,818,826,833,840,819,837,822,831,869]
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] Even spread: all 12 partitions share the load.
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — BankPartitioner ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Strategy: Partitioner is pluggable (default / custom bucketed)   │
  │   WHY: swap key strategy without changing the producer           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: partitioner only maps key→partition                           │
  │ O: new strategy (composite key) = new Partitioner, no edits      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │     BankPartitioner      │
  │  - numPartitions: int    │
  │  + partitionFor(key):int │
  │  - murmur2(bytes):int    │
  └──────────────────────────┘
            uses key from
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │        Transfer          │
  │  - accountId, region     │
  │  - amount: BigDecimal    │
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── Contract for partitionFor(key) ─────────────────────────
    Pre:  numPartitions > 0
    Post: returns value in [0, numPartitions)
    Rule: same key always returns same partition (ordering)

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. producer.send("transfers", accountId, event)
  2.   → partitioner.partitionFor(accountId)
  3.   → murmur2(accountId) & 0x7fffffff % 12
  4.   → append to that partition's log
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Choosing a partition key is about balancing two things: ordering and distribution. Kafka hashes the key and takes it modulo the partition count to pick a partition, and records with the same key always land in the same partition, which is what gives you per-key ordering. In a bank, I key by account id, because there are millions of accounts with roughly even traffic, so load spreads across all partitions while every account's debits and credits stay in order on one partition.

A bad key is one with low cardinality or heavy skew, like region, status, or a boolean flag. If ninety percent of my traffic is from one region and I key by region, that one value hashes to a single partition and roughly ninety percent of records pile into it. That is a hot partition. Because a partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in a group, the consumer on the hot partition falls far behind while the others sit idle, the broker leading that partition runs hot on CPU and disk, and adding more consumers does not help because you cannot subdivide a single partition.

The symptoms I watch for are one partition's lag climbing while the rest stay near zero, and one broker showing much higher load than its peers. When I genuinely have a single dominant key that I cannot split, there are senior techniques: a composite key like account id plus a small bucket number to fan one very active account across a few partitions, a custom partitioner that routes known high-volume accounts to dedicated partitions, or increasing partitions when the skew is spread across many keys rather than one. The caution is that any time I loosen the key for distribution, I may lose per-account ordering, so I only do it where the ordering change is tolerable.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, we originally keyed the transfers topic by region and created a textbook hot partition, with one partition holding the bulk of the records and its consumer lagging badly while the others were empty. We switched the key to account id, the load immediately spread evenly across all twelve partitions, lag dropped, and we kept per-account ordering. The senior framing I give is that the key is not just a technical detail; it is a design decision that simultaneously controls correctness through ordering and performance through distribution, and getting it wrong wastes a cluster that has plenty of partitions but can only go as fast as its hottest one.
